items.summary: 活动报名｜MEET2027最新嘉宾阵容，12月9日北京见！ DDPM Gen AI DL 量子位 2026-11-19 18:20 分享 以下文章来源于mp.weixin.qq.com MEET组委会 发自 凹非寺 量子位 | 公众号QbitAI 2026年，AI领域最显著的变化发生在交付现场：模型开始接手任务，机器人离开舞台走进产线，智能体被嵌进组织的日常流程。这些事分散在不同行业与场景里，我们却从中看到了同一条线索。 12月9日，量子位主办的 MEET2027智能未来大会 将在北京·金茂万丽酒店举行。 学术、产业、投资 不同方向上的一线实践者，将在这里共同来回答：当AI从模型能力变成可交付的系统产出，是谁在把它送进真实场景，又是谁在底层为它提供支撑？ 来MEET2027现场，来听这些问题的完整答案🔽 当前16位重磅嘉宾已确认 王颖 百度集团副总裁 个人超级智能事业群组总裁 王颖女士，毕业于北京科技大学管理学院，随后获得中欧国际工商学院EMBA学位，曾任搜狗公司高级副总裁，现任百度集团副总裁、个人超级智能事业群组总裁。 2021年加入百度后，王颖女士全面负责包括百度文库在内的百度互娱和垂类业务。2024年至今，王颖女士全面负责百度文库、百度网盘、百度学术等关键业务。2026年，百度成立个人超级智能事业群组，由王颖女士挂帅，持续引领百度文库、百度网盘的发展及库库、KOOKO等产品创新和落地。 方汉 昆仑万维董事长兼CEO 毕业于中国科学技术大学近代物理系，曾任职于中国科学院高能物理研究所、拓林思、亚信以及千橡互动，2008年3月协助周亚辉先生创立昆仑万维。 方汉先生拥有30年互联网从业经验，从1994年开始参与和倡导开源运动，是中文Linux奠基人、中文Linux四剑客之一，著作国内第一本Linux书籍《Linux实用大全》；也是国内最早的网络安全专家，曾负责三大电信运营商的全网安全审计，领导开发了国内第一款P2P下载软件DUDU加速器，负责研发了国内市场占有率最高的网页游戏《三国风云》，为中国互联网最资深的参与者。 王金桥 中国科学院自动化研究所副总工程师 紫东太初大模型研究中心主任 中科紫东太初董事长 武汉人工智能研究院院长，中科紫东太初董事长，中国科学院大学人工智能学院岗位教授；兼任多模态人工智能产业联盟秘书长、工信部人工智能标委会WG7智能产品与服务组长，长
items.content: 活动报名｜MEET2027最新嘉宾阵容，12月9日北京见！ DDPM Gen AI DL 量子位 2026-11-19 18:20 分享 以下文章来源于mp.weixin.qq.com MEET组委会 发自 凹非寺 量子位 | 公众号QbitAI 2026年，AI领域最显著的变化发生在交付现场：模型开始接手任务，机器人离开舞台走进产线，智能体被嵌进组织的日常流程。这些事分散在不同行业与场景里，我们却从中看到了同一条线索。 12月9日，量子位主办的 MEET2027智能未来大会 将在北京·金茂万丽酒店举行。 学术、产业、投资 不同方向上的一线实践者，将在这里共同来回答：当AI从模型能力变成可交付的系统产出，是谁在把它送进真实场景，又是谁在底层为它提供支撑？ 来MEET2027现场，来听这些问题的完整答案🔽 当前16位重磅嘉宾已确认 王颖 百度集团副总裁 个人超级智能事业群组总裁 王颖女士，毕业于北京科技大学管理学院，随后获得中欧国际工商学院EMBA学位，曾任搜狗公司高级副总裁，现任百度集团副总裁、个人超级智能事业群组总裁。 2021年加入百度后，王颖女士全面负责包括百度文库在内的百度互娱和垂类业务。2024年至今，王颖女士全面负责百度文库、百度网盘、百度学术等关键业务。2026年，百度成立个人超级智能事业群组，由王颖女士挂帅，持续引领百度文库、百度网盘的发展及库库、KOOKO等产品创新和落地。 方汉 昆仑万维董事长兼CEO 毕业于中国科学技术大学近代物理系，曾任职于中国科学院高能物理研究所、拓林思、亚信以及千橡互动，2008年3月协助周亚辉先生创立昆仑万维。 方汉先生拥有30年互联网从业经验，从1994年开始参与和倡导开源运动，是中文Linux奠基人、中文Linux四剑客之一，著作国内第一本Linux书籍《Linux实用大全》；也是国内最早的网络安全专家，曾负责三大电信运营商的全网安全审计，领导开发了国内第一款P2P下载软件DUDU加速器，负责研发了国内市场占有率最高的网页游戏《三国风云》，为中国互联网最资深的参与者。 王金桥 中国科学院自动化研究所副总工程师 紫东太初大模型研究中心主任 中科紫东太初董事长 武汉人工智能研究院院长，中科紫东太初董事长，中国科学院大学人工智能学院岗位教授；兼任多模态人工智能产业联盟秘书长、工信部人工智能标委会WG7智能产品与服务组长，长期从事多模态大模型、视频理解与检索、大规模视觉识别研究，是国内多模态通用大模型领域权威专家，2025福布斯中国“人工智能影响力人物”。 累计在IEEE系列权威期刊和国际顶级会议发表论文300余篇，其中期刊论文50余篇、国际顶会论文220余篇；牵头推动国家标准提案13项，获授权发明专利36项，10次获国际顶级视觉算法竞赛冠军。先后获世界人工智能大会SAIL卓越引领者奖、吴文俊人工智能科技进步二等奖、北京市科技进步一等奖、北京市自然科学二等奖、湖北省科技进步二等奖、中国发明创新银奖、祖冲之奖、新时代中国经济创新人物等，入选中国科学院“科苑名匠”团队。 方跃 中欧国际工商学院AI与管理创新研究中心主任 深圳市硅基管理创新研究院创始执行院长 方跃教授，中欧国际工商学院AI与管理创新研究中心主任、深圳市硅基管理创新研究院创始执行院长。方教授获麻省理工学院决策科学博士、运筹学硕士及清华大学应用数学学士学位。他长期深耕AI组织变革、企业数智化转型与管理决策创新，兼具国际学术研究、硅谷金融及企业战略咨询经验。他曾发起成立中欧数字经济与智慧企业研究中心，并牵头创办中欧AI与管理创新研究中心，聚焦企业从AI工具应用走向AI原生组织的演进路径，推动管理理论、转型方法与产业实践融合。他著有《数字化领导力》《超级智体：企业未来的无限进化》《超级智体启动指南：企业AI转型行动手册》等，也持续为科技、高端制造、汽车及金融等行业的AI转型提供研究与实践支持。 许锦波 分子 之心创始人 国际计算生物学会（ISCB） Fellow 被业界誉为“AI蛋白质折叠奠基人”，在生物计算领域深耕20余年，一直致力于用AI算法解决蛋白 质结构预测、优化、设计等问题，取得了众多从0到1的全球性原创突破成果，不仅做出开先河式的学术突破，也将AI蛋白质技术推向产业应用，对学术界和工业界 带来了广泛且深刻的影响。 作为全球AI蛋白质结构预测领域的领军人物，许教授于2016年发明RaptorX-Contact方法，全球首次证明AI可以大幅提升蛋白质结构预测精度，在蛋白质结构预测这一有六十多年历史的世界难题上取得了实质性的进展。 许教授曾获多项国际顶级奖项，包括美国斯隆研究奖、美国自然科学基金早期职业奖、国际计算生物学官方期刊《PLoS Computational Biology》创新突破奖、国际计算生物学顶级会议RECOMB最佳论文奖和时间检验奖、首届国际基础科学大会前沿科学奖等。2022年作为唯一中国大陆代表，参加诺贝尔基金会关于“人类3D蛋白质组”的专题研讨会。 顾进杰 蚂蚁健康事业群CTO 百灵医疗大模型负责人 顾进杰，蚂蚁健康事业群CTO，百灵医疗大模型负责人。硕士毕业于南京大学，带领团队推动医疗AGI和创新产品研发。25年阿福APP进入中国AGI原生APP MAU规模Top5，26年阿福获得《时代》杂志“最佳发明”。团队发布了蚂蚁安诊儿开源医疗大模型，并推动医疗健康系列的评测、训推技术的开源。 在蚂蚁先后负责过人工智能部、支付宝等部门的核心AI应用落地，团队累计在国际AI顶会NeurIPS、ICLR、ICML、SIGKDD等累计发表超过50篇论文，两次获得“吴文俊”人工智能科技进步奖一等奖，两次获得WAIC世界人工智能大会SAIL奖，两次获得世界互联网大会年度领先科技奖。 王云鹤 基元律动创始人兼CEO 西安电子科技大学本科、北京大学智能科学系博士，发表论文200余篇，谷歌学术引用超4万次。曾任华为诺亚方舟实验室主任。2026年4月创办基元律动，提出“Agent = Base Models + Harness”，推出OpenSquilla运行时、NeoHorse-1系列模型及TokenRhythm API平台。 夏立雪 无问芯穹联合创始人兼首席执行官 学士与博士均毕业于清华大学电子工程系。在夏立雪的带领下，无问芯穹已发展成为AI基础设施领域最具代表性的高新技术企业之一。他连续五年入选斯坦福全球学科Top2%科学家榜单、连续两年入选AI2000人工智能全球最具影响力学者榜单（芯片方向Top100），任上海市徐汇区第十七届人大代表、第十一届青联委员，获2025年全国工业和信息化系统劳动模范、宁夏算力枢纽人工智能领域领军人才、2025央视年度十大AI人物、2025财富40U40商业精英、2024福布斯中国新时代颠覆力创始人、36氪WISE2024商业之王新世代先锋等表彰。 夏立雪长期致力于人工智能系统的设计方法学研究，已发表30余篇学术论文，谷歌学术引用3500余次。他在大语言模型的压缩加速、生成式AI模型芯片等领域的相关工作，是世界首个面向深度学习语音合成领域的定制化硬件设计，在国际上处于领先地位。 洪源 太初（杭州）集成电路有限公司首席产品官兼高级副总裁 现任太初元碁首席产品官、高级副总裁，兼任发改委人工智能智库专家、中国自动化学会自主指令集专委委员等社会职务。拥有多年AI行业管理经验，曾参与《多元融合智能算力技术白皮书（2024年）》、《人工智能芯片云侧推理用深度学习芯片测试指标与测试方法》2022-0589T-SJ行业标准等多个行业标准与白皮书撰写。 金贻荣 相干科技创始人兼CEO 北京量子院生态建设团队负责人 金贻荣博士，相干科技创始人兼CEO、北京量子院生态建设团队负责人及超导量子计算领域科研负责人。毕业于中国科学技术大学，获凝聚态物理与电子信息工程双学士学位，后获中国科学院物理研究所凝聚态物理学博士学位，师从张殿琳院士。 长期致力于量子计算核心技术研发与产业化，推动芯片设计制造、测控系统集成、整机研制及云平台建设全链条协同发展，积极促进技术成果转化与产业生态建设。现任全国量子计算与测量标准化技术委员会（SAC/TC578）委员、中国通信学会量子计算委员会委员、中国计算机学会量子计算专业委员会执行委员。 姚远 面壁智能学术合伙人 联席首席科学家 面壁智能联席首席科学家、清华大学人工智能学院助理教授，领衔面壁智能多模态大模型实验室、具身智能实验室。在Nature Communications、CVPR、ACL、ICML等顶会顶刊发表论文30余篇，谷歌学术引用1万余次。主导构建MiniCPM-V、MiniCPM-o等高效多模态模型，连续多天在HuggingFace Trending和GitHub Trending排名第一。开源项目总星标3.9万余次，模型总下载量超4000万次。曾获吴文俊人工智能科学技术奖优秀博士学位论文奖、英特尔中国学术成就奖、世界人工智能大会云帆奖、中关村论坛年会10项重大科技成果等荣誉。 宣善明 商汤科技大装置事业群副总裁、CTO 毕业于北京大学电子学系本硕，现任商汤科技大装置事业群副总裁、CTO，负责产品研发、SRE及客户服务体系，推动算力、平台与模型服务一体化发展，支撑万卡至十万卡级大模型训练与推理。主导国产算力异构混合推理（PD分离）架构创新与规模化商业落地，推动国产异构算力从技术验证走向生产级交付，构建日均10万亿Token产能的端到端Token工厂生态体系。此前任职于微软AI Platform首席研发经理，拥有12年微软工作经历，深耕大模型训练与推理基础设施，具备万卡级集群管理、十万卡异构调度及高吞吐优化经验，曾参与Azure OpenAI全球资源调度及Microsoft 365 Copilot平台的产品设计与研发。 廖文龙 酷哇科技创始人兼首席技术官 上海交通大学博士，机器人算法与系统领域专家，2015年联合创立酷哇科技，长期担任公司核心技术负责人。曾主导设计多款消费级及工业级机器人，推动AI机器人研发与量产，持续深耕机器人从核心算法、软硬件平台到AI基础设施的全栈技术研发，推动公司「一脑多形」技术体系及多场景具身智能机器人的规模化落地。在CVPR、AAAI等国际学术会议及期刊发表论文20篇，拥有发明专利237项。 周而进 原力灵机联合创始人、CTO 原力灵机联合创始人兼首席技术官，负责公司基础模型研发及AI基础设施开发。毕业于清华大学电子工程系，曾获国际信息学奥林匹克（IOI）金牌。加入原力灵机前，他曾任旷视科研院轮值院长、旷视人脸算法负责人及深度学习训练框架天元（MegEngine）负责人。周而进长期从事计算机视觉、人工智能及机器人研发与产品落地，曾带领团队在NIST FRVT、中国首届人工智能大赛人脸组等多项国内外评测与竞赛中取得冠军，相关AI技术已应用于手机、智能相机、机器人等多类产品，覆盖超过千万台AIoT设备。 陆弘远 脸谱心智创始人 香港中文大学博士，本科硕士毕业于英国帝国理工大学。曾作为第一作者代表亚洲机构首次作为独立机构获得ACL旗下旗舰会议最佳论文奖，作者仅两人，无公司背景。Adam's 刘闯，第六镜科技创始人、CEO，西北工业大学控制科学与工程专业博士研究生，2019年福布斯中国30位30岁以下精英榜入选者、西安市首批领军型青年企业家。2014年在校期间创立第六镜科技，专注计算机视觉、工业大模型与智能系统的研发及产业化，探索人工智能与物理世界的融合。 他带领团队构建从AI核心工具链、标准化软硬件产品到行业应用的技术产品体系，以工业质检、安全生产等复杂场景为切入点，牵头研发Prismind系列工业视觉检测装备及管道内壁检测机器人，推动成果在河钢、太钢、中国石油等企业落地。目前探索智能体与具身智能的应用，推动AI从识别感知走向决策执行与闭环管理。面向未来，他致力于将工业现场积累的技术能力与工程经验沉淀为可复用的产品与应用能力，拓展至千行百业，推动“AI+”从技术探索走向规模化应用。 以上展示顺序不分先后，更多重磅嘉宾正在陆续确认中，敬请期待。 席位有限，报名从速！ MEET智能未来大会是量子位年度最具代表性的科技商业峰会，每年汇聚 上千名 科技从业者 到场， 百万 观众 线上参与， 近百家合作媒体 联合曝光，被视为智能科技行业的年度风向标。 参会者能带走的，不只是台上的观点。全天议程之外，大会留出了充足的交流时间——嘉宾、同行与产业伙伴之间的对话，不止在聚光灯下，更在会场之外的走廊里。 聚变正在发生：技术路线在收敛，产业格局在重排，投资逻辑在换挡。 三线交汇之处，正是破局所在。 席位有限，建议尽快报名，与我们一起在12月9日的大会现场预见智能新篇。 大会时间 ：12月9日 大会地点 ：北京·金茂万丽酒店 大会主题 ：智行合一·驭见未来 items.content: Lean verification of the Riemann Hypothesis Joint statement by the Lean and Mathlib communities, endorsed by the Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative. On November 20, 2026, Levent Alpöge released a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis as a Lean library comprising 17 million lines of code. We have full confidence that Alpöge's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement. Our rationale is outlined below. The codebase depends directly only on Mathlib. Over the past day, the Lean and Mathlib communities have rallied to verify the proof's correctness. We hereby certify that both the statement and the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis are correct. The four criteria in https://xenaproject.wordpress.com/2026/11/12/and-the-proof-is-checked-in-lean/ are all satisfied. The statement of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct. This statement is part of Mathlib: RiemannHypothesis and has been carefully vetted by experts in Lean and number theory. Alpöge’s library compiles correctly. By now, dozens of people have reported correct compilation of the codebase, reproducing the same raw proof export file. The library compiles without errors or build failures. The code proves the correct statement. Crucially, the community has added a file that isolates the statement of the Riemann Hypothesis and imports only Mathlib. That statement was compared against the theorem proved by Alpöge using two independent tools ( comparator and con-leche –compare ), both confirming that the theorem proved in Alpöge’s library is exactly Mathlib’s statement of the Riemann Hypothesis. The Lean proof is valid. The exported raw proof has been checked by several proof checkers, including Lean’s official kernel, the con-leche and con-ron checkers, and several independent checkers contributed by third parties and implemented in different programming languages. The checkers con-leche and con-ron come with a formal proof, relative to set theory, that they cannot accept a false proof, thus addressing concerns that Lean’s logic itself might have flaws that the proof could exploit. An extensive overview is available at https://math.mit.edu/~drew/grh/ . These checks ran on an inert export of the proof, out of reach of hypothetical malicious code in the Lean proof sources. Thanks are owed to everyone in the community who provided resources for the verification. We look forward to all the activity in the mathematical community that will help explain the new ideas in this proof.

items.content: Algorithms and theory Google’s mission presents many exciting algorithmic and optimization challenges across different product areas including Search, Ads, Social, and Google Infrastructure. These include optimizing internal systems such as scheduling the machines that power the numerous computations done each day, as well as optimizations that affect core products and users, from online allocation of ads to page-views to automatic management of ad campaigns, and from clustering large-scale graphs to finding best paths in transportation networks. Other than employing new algorithmic ideas to impact millions of users, Google researchers contribute to the state-of-the-art research in these areas by publishing in top conferences and journals. Recent Publications See More Depth-CoT Tradeoffs in Transformers: A Look at Path Following Clayton Sanford Matus Telgarsky Justin D. Li 2027 Preview Preview abstract Modern transformers have been scaled up in size, data, training-time compute, and more recently test-time compute based on Chain-of-Thought (CoT), but the consequences of trading off these parameters are unknown. We construct explicit tradeoffs between two of these aspects: the number of layers in a transformer and the number of CoT tokens. Our first result is general: with mild assumptions and a single-token prompt, for any integer k, a transformer using soft attention and SwiGLU MLP layers with L layers and n CoT tokens can be converted to a transformer with at most ckL layers and ⌈n/k⌉ CoT tokens, and vice versa, although with an increase to the size of other parameters. We then a multi-token prompt path following task, finding that additional preprocessing from the multi-token prompt changes the depth-CoT relationship in this case. We construct an attention-only network with L layers and 2^(L−2) heads that can traverse 2^(L−1) − 1 edges along a path with a single CoT token, demonstrating at least an exponential relationship between increases in depth and reductions in the number of CoT tokens needed to traverse the entire path. This relationship for the path following task holds empirically as well, as demonstrated by training networks with up to 5 layers, with the tradeoff between depth and the maximum number of edge traversals in a single CoT token exactly matching our theoretical constructions. View details Geo-Contextual AI Concierge: Minimizing Internal Support Friction Through Proactive Knowledge Synthesis Neeraj Choudhary Dónal Doyle Technical Report (2026) Preview Preview abstract In large-scale distributed enterprises, traditional Knowledge Management (KM) systems face a critical failure mode: static documentation cannot keep pace with evolving operational realities and regional nuances. This "knowledge latency" forces employees out of self-service workflows and into costly support ticketing queues. This paper introduces SENTINEL, a geo-contextual AI framework designed to shift enterprise support from reactive retrieval to proactive interception. The architecture employs a novel dual-engine system integrated into an omni-present interface. The first engine utilizes Large Language Models (LLMs) to conduct pre-emptive, historical case-grounded audits of documentation, generating a "Contextual Density" score that identifies friction zones. The second engine is an autonomous Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) agent that surfaces in-situ via a location-intelligent assistant window, resolving queries in real-time. By functioning as a strategic "defensive barrier" at the point of origin, SENTINEL demonstrates how a proactive AI assistant can drive high-fidelity, in-situ case deflection. View details Rational Transductors Mehryar Mohri ICML 2026 Preview Preview abstract Standard Transformers excel at semantic modeling but struggle with rigid sequential logic and state tracking, fundamentally limited to AC0 complexity without intermediate chain-of- thought. In this work, we introduce Rational Transductors, a dual-stream architecture that augments the Transformer with a linear, matrix-valued recurrence derived from Weighted Finite Automata (WFA). By injecting rational state information into the attention mechanism via a Deep Rational Injection scheme, our framework strictly generalizes the expressive power of Transformers to capture all Regular Languages and NC1-complete problems (such as Parity and Modular Counting) while preserving O(log T) parallel training efficiency. View details Distributional Alignment Games for Answer-Level Fine-Tuning Mehryar Mohri Jon Schneider Yifan Wu ICML 2026 Preview Preview abstract We focus on the problem of \emph{Answer-Level Fine-Tuning} (ALFT), where the goal is to optimize a language model based on the correctness or properties of its final answers, rather than the specific reasoning traces used to produce them. Directly optimizing answer-level objectives is computationally intractable due to the need to marginalize over the vast space of latent reasoning paths. To overcome this, we propose a general game-theoretical framework that lifts the problem to a \emph{Distributional Alignment Game}. We formulate ALFT as a two-player game between a Policy (the generator) and a Target (an auxiliary distribution). We prove that the Nash Equilibrium of this game corresponds exactly to the solution of the original answer-level optimization problem. View details Cardio Load in exercise and everyday life: A modified TRIMP metric for continuously-sensing consumer wearables Justin Phillips Daniel Roggen YongSuk Cho Robert Harle Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise (2026) Preview Preview abstract PURPOSE: To introduce Cardio Load (CL), a metric quantifying cardiovascular work from all activities across the day, and to investigate its distribution by age, gender, and workout profiles. CL adapts the Training Impulse (TRIMP) model by leveraging continuous heart rate and movement data from wearables, enabling minute-level intensity estimation. We also discuss the derivation of weekly target loads, intended to guide fitness maintenance. METHODS: A retrospective analysis was conducted on 31.2 million hours of wrist-worn wearable data collected over a six-week period. The dataset comprised a 40,000-subject subset (37.9% female) of consenting Google Pixel Watch® users in the United States, aged 18 to 80 years (18-39: 41.8%, 40-59: 43.5%, 60+: 14.6%). Measured data included minute-interval heart rate averages, resting and maximum heart rates, minute-interval averaged accelerometer log energy, and manually-logged or auto-detected activity types. Cardio Load scores and target loads were calculated daily for each subject and compared across age and gender. We also compared the proportions of CL gained during workouts and incidental daily activities for these groups. RESULTS: Overall, the study population's mean ± SD weekly CL scores were 221 ± 156 (female) and 259 ± 169 (male). Median weekly Cardio Load (CL) values exhibited consistency for individuals between 30 and 75 years of age. When analyzed in five-year age groups, the coefficient of variation (CV%) of median weekly CL values within this age range was less than 4.5%, with younger and older subjects demonstrating higher and lower median CL, respectively. The median proportion of CL accumulated during structured workouts versus incidental daily activity was 41.0% (female) and 49.0% (male) for all subjects, though this varied considerably with average weekly workout duration. CV% of weekly target load and daily target load over 6 weeks was 23.6% and 35.2% respectively. CONCLUSION: Cardio Load provides a continuous quantification of activity load from wearables, acknowledging both structured workouts and everydayincidental activity. CL is equitably rewarded for age ranges spanning 30-75 years. Weekly target loads were found to have little measurement variability and be more consistent and, consequently, more practical for planning training and physical activity than daily targets. View details Marginalized Bundle Adjustment: Multi-View Camera Pose from Monocular Depth Estimates Shengjie Zhu Ahmed Abdelkader Mark Matthews Xiaoming Liu Vincent Chu International Conference on 3D Vision (2026) Preview Preview abstract Structure-from-Motion (SfM) is a classical 3D vision task for recovering camera parameters and scene geometry from multi-view images. Recent advances in deep learning enable accurate monocular depth estimation (MDE) that infers structure from a single image without depending on camera motion. But integrating MDE into SfM remains challenging. Unlike classical triangulated sparse pointclouds, MDE produces dense depthmaps with significantly higher error variance. Inspired by modern RANSAC estimators, we propose a Marginalized Bundle Adjustment (MBA) to accommodate MDE error variance with its density. With MBA, we show that MDE depthmaps are sufficiently accurate to support SoTA or competitive results in Structure-from-Motion and camera relocalization. Our benchmark demonstrates consistent remarkable results from two-view, few-frames small multiview, to thousands-frames large multiview system. Our method highlights the significant potential of MDE on multi-view 3D vision tasks. items.content: Back to Articles Hugging Face and OpenRouter join forces to make open-weight models easy to run Published November 16, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 115 +109 Célina Hanouti celinah Follow Victor Mustar victor Follow Bertrand Chevrier kramp Follow Lucain Pouget Wauplin Follow Pierric Cistac pierric Follow Eliott Coyac coyotte508 Follow Julien Chaumond julien-c Follow Hugging Face and OpenRouter are teaming up to make open-weight models easy to run. Every major open-weight release is already being published on the Hugging Face Hub, and OpenRouter serves those models at scale, routing each request across 80+ providers based on live measurements of each one. Together, every open-weight model on the Hub that a provider serves can be called with your Hugging Face token, through the same API, with the best provider picked for each request. Today, we are switching Inference Providers from our own custom router to OpenRouter's. Requests made to language models now go through OpenRouter, which picks the best provider for each call based on live price, speed and reliability, and retries on another provider if the first one fails. Your code stays the same. Run them with the tools you already use The router supports OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs and Anthropic's Messages API for every chat model, whatever the provider behind it. Pick your coding agent or SDK and a model, then copy the steps, or copy the whole setup as a prompt for your agent: Setup guides for Claude Code , Codex , OpenCode , Pi and Hermes Agent The same Hugging Face token also gives you storage with Storage Buckets , compute with Jobs and dedicated inference with Inference Endpoints . PRO, Team and Enterprise plans include monthly credits for compute and inference. How open-weight models are used On OpenRouter, open-weight models went from 26.8% of the tokens served in October 2025 to 71.7% at the end of September 2026, after peaking at 77.5% in July ( OpenRouter, October 2026 ). Over the same period, weekly open-weight volume grew more than 60-fold, against almost tenfold for closed models. This week, the most used model on OpenRouter is an open-weight one, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, with 59.2 trillion tokens ( rankings ). Open-weight models cost about four times less on average: $0.28 per million input tokens and $1.62 per million output tokens, against $1.27 and $6.36 for closed models. The best open-weight models still trail the best proprietary ones on the hardest benchmarks. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index , Kimi K3.1 Pro, the best open-weight model, scores 46 against 65 for Claude Fable 5.2, at about a seventh of the cost per task ($3.68 against $26.54). For a lot of workloads, that trade-off is worth it. Routing powered by OpenRouter OpenRouter serves more than 800 trillion tokens a month to over 10 million users, across 600+ models from 80+ providers. Its routing is based on live measurements of every provider across that traffic. OpenRouter recently rebuilt its provider routing : instead of only looking at the lowest list price, it sends each request to the provider with the best mix of price, speed and reliability. When a provider slows down or starts failing, traffic moves away from it until it recovers, and a failed try is retried on the next best provider inside the same call. In OpenRouter's measurements, the new routing cut capacity errors by 46% and improved time to first token by 16.9% and throughput by 16.3%. Before, Inference Providers picked one provider for your request and returned its error if it failed. Now, the request is retried on another provider. You can still choose a policy or a provider with a suffix on the model id: zai-org/GLM-5.3 # default: best mix of price, speed and reliability zai-org/GLM-5.3:fastest # highest throughput zai-org/GLM-5.3:cheapest # lowest price zai-org/GLM-5.3:novita # only Novita Routing is also cache-aware: a conversation stays on the provider that holds its prompt cache. To make it explicit, send a stable UUID per conversation in the X-HF-Session-Id header (see the prompt caching guide ). Pricing Pricing doesn't change: you pay the provider's price on your Hugging Face bill, and Hugging Face doesn't add a markup on top of it. PRO users get $2 of credits every month, and Team and Enterprise organizations get $2 per seat. See Pricing and Billing for the details. Image, video and audio generation Image, video, and audio generation continue to work exactly as before, directly through Hugging Face Inference Providers without going through OpenRouter. You can keep using the same token and API, and access tens of thousands of LoRAs . See where your requests go On model pages, you can chat with the model right away in the widget. Two new tabs show what's behind it: Providers lists every provider OpenRouter can route the model to, with its input and output price, speed and uptime over the last 24 hours, and Metrics shows the best price, throughput, time to first token, context length and uptime among them: Your usage overview breaks your spend down by the provider each request went to: In your settings , you can turn off any provider you don't want: the router never sends your requests there. Organizations have the same settings, and they apply to every request billed to the organization. Breaking change: custom provider keys Requests to language models now go through OpenRouter and are billed to your Hugging Face account or organization, so you can no longer use your own API key for a provider with these models. You can still pick a provider with a suffix on the model id ( model:provider ) or turn providers off in your settings, and your code stays the same. Custom keys for image and video providers keep working. What's next This is the first step of our partnership with OpenRouter. Next: Connect your OpenRouter account to Hugging Face. More tasks routed through OpenRouter. Try a model , or read the Inference Providers docs to get started. More Articles from our Blog llms inference-providers baseten Baseten on Hugging Face Inference Providers 🔥 +4 34 August 6, 2026 llms inference-providers deepinfra DeepInfra on Hugging Face Inference Providers 🔥 +4 15 April 29, 2026 Community pnayakus 4 days ago Hi, I wanted to know if we have hugging face pretrained model why we have to redo model from scratch for any system? Can we use Hugging face any model online and use in our programs? Thanks. See translation Reply Pauliehedron 4 days ago • edited 4 days ago Does your version follow the cache-hit price or does it force us to keep constantly watching and blocking providers who game the input and output pricing to harvest the cache-hit and the full cache-miss? Because openrouter themselves you have to have a full non fine grained admin key and monitor yourself or else put in guardrails and lock to providers or put in your own local proxies to do the monitoring with the admin key. Which is quite a burden for a service taking a 5:5% cut like openrouter does. Are you doing the same??? You can still choose a policy or a provider with a suffix on the model id: zai-org/GLM-5.3 # default: best mix of price, speed and reliability zai-org/GLM-5.3:fastest # highest throughput zai-org/GLM-5.3:cheapest # lowest price zai-org/GLM-5.3:novita # only Novita Routing is also cache-aware: a conversation stays on the provider that holds its prompt cache. To make it explicit, send a stable UUID per conversation in the X-HF-Session-Id header (see the prompt caching guide ). Pricing Pricing doesn't change: you pay the provider's price on your Hugging Face bill, and Hugging Face doesn't add a markup on top of it. PRO users get $2 of credits every month, and Team and Enterprise organizations get $2 per seat. See Pricing and Billing for the details. Image, video and audio generation Image, video, and audio generation continue to work exactly as before, directly through Hugging Face Inference Providers without going through OpenRouter. You can keep using the same token and API, and access tens of thousands of LoRAs . See where your requests go On model pages, you can chat with the model right away in the widget. Two new tabs show what's behind it: Providers lists every provider OpenRouter can route the model to, with its input and output price, speed and uptime over the last 24 hours, and Metrics shows the best price, throughput, time to first token, context length and uptime among them: Your usage overview breaks your spend down by the provider each request went to: In your settings , you can turn off any provider you don't want: the router never sends your requests there. Organizations have the same settings, and they apply to every request billed to the organization. Breaking change: custom provider keys Requests to language models now go through OpenRouter and are billed to your Hugging Face account or organization, so you can no longer use your own API key for a provider with these models. You can still pick a provider with a suffix on the model id ( model:provider ) or turn providers off in your settings, and your code stays the same. Custom keys for image and video providers keep working. What's next This is the first step of our partnership with OpenRouter. Next: Connect your OpenRouter account to Hugging Face. More tasks routed through OpenRouter. Try a model , or read the Inference Providers docs to get started. items.content: Back to Articles DaisyRose-27B: Pushing the Frontier of Post-Training Efficiency Team Article Published November 18, 2026 Upvote 29 +23 Jason Chen jzsc Follow RadixArk Today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B , RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles . We trained it on long-horizon agent tasks with sessions up to 1M tokens, with just 1,200 curated tasks in 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs. DaisyRose-27B improves Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 from 5.6% to 12.0% . Beyond Terminal-Bench 4.1, it also delivers gains on a variety of other reasoning, instruction following, and coding benchmarks. The checkpoints are available under Apache 2.0 : BF16 FP8 NVFP4 The model retains Qwen3.8-27B’s architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window . The longer training sessions use harness summarization to span multiple trajectories. See the model card for model properties and inference settings. Run DaisyRose-27B We recommend serving DaisyRose-27B with SGLang and DSpark speculative decoding. The SGLang cookbook provides launch configurations for different GPUs and checkpoint formats. After starting the server with the served model name DaisyRose-27B on port 30000 , you can send a request using the OpenAI Python client: from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI( base_url= "http://localhost:30000/v1" , api_key= "none" , ) response = client.chat.completions.create( model= "DaisyRose-27B" , messages=[ { "role" : "user" , "content" : "How many positive divisors does 360 have?" , } ], temperature= 1.0 , top_p= 0.95 , extra_body={ "top_k" : 20 , "min_p" : 0.0 }, ) print (response.choices[ 0 ].message.reasoning_content) print (response.choices[ 0 ].message.content) The model thinks before answering by default. Its reasoning is returned in reasoning_content , and its final answer in content . These settings follow the model card’s quickstart . Benchmark results Benchmark Qwen3.8-27B DaisyRose-27B Terminal Bench 4.1 5.6 12.0 Terminal Bench 2.1 73.0 75.5 DeepSWE v1.1 42.2 46.2 SWE Bench Pro v2 91.3 94.7 HLE (text-only) 33.9 34.3 IFBench 79.5 82.4 GPQA Diamond 89.2 90.7 DaisyRose-27B scores higher than the original Qwen3.8-27B model on every benchmark above. The largest gain is on Terminal Bench 4.1, where pass@1 rises from 5.6% to 12.0%. Scores use the higher of the BF16 and FP8 runs for each benchmark; the two differ by less than one point wherever both were evaluated. The model card includes comparison sources and evaluation settings. Three parts of the training setup made this release possible: carefully designed tasks, an efficient training backend, and reliable sandboxes. High-quality training data We built the tasks in partnership with Eigent AI , starting from its large pool of tasks in machine learning, software engineering, science, and other fields. Together we built thousands of candidates. About 1,200 made it into the final training set. We selected tasks using three criteria: Each task targets a mistake the original model makes. We ran Qwen3.8-27B on every task and redesigned each one around the mistakes we wanted the model to stop making. We then adjusted the difficulty until the solve rate fell within a useful learning range. Each task requires several interdependent steps. The agent has to reason, plan, and execute across a long job. Each attempt gets up to 1.5 hours in a sandbox, with more than 100 tool calls and more than 256K output tokens. Tasks must reward actually solving the problem. We reviewed every task alongside the model’s attempts. Tasks that could be passed without solving the intended problem, or that contained a design flaw, were fixed or removed. Efficient training backend RadixArk trained DaisyRose-27B with Miles, our open-source reinforcement learning framework for large-scale model post-training, in fully asynchronous mode: the agent keeps working while the model learns, and neither waits for the other. While 128 H200s run the inference on agent tasks, 16 more run the trainer and learn from the trajectories. After every step, the updated model goes out to the 128 GPUs that run the agent. The learning runs on our internal training backend, which is built for agent training: each step learns from a handful of very long sessions, some as long as 1M tokens, folded into multiple trajectories via harness summarization. 57% lower training cost. On this release, 37% of each GPU’s peak compute went into useful training work (model FLOPs utilization, or MFU) on our backend. The open-source trainer, built on Megatron, reached 16% on comparable runs. So the same training needs 57% less GPU time. The gain is even larger on mixture-of-experts models: 6.2× on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and more than 10× on the roughly 300B-parameter GLM-5.3-Flash. 2× faster end to end. Counting the time the agent spends on its tasks, the release run trained on about 16,800 tokens per second across its 144 GPUs. The open-source trainer reached about 8,300 on the same GPUs. Stable over weeks. The release run trained for weeks on 144 H200s, 63,000 GPU-hours in total. From the first step to the last, its speed and efficiency held steady. Every training step of the DaisyRose-27B release run on 144 H200s, plotted against total training time. Dashed lines: the open-source trainer on comparable runs. Robust sandbox service Every training attempt runs in a sandbox: a fresh copy of the task’s environment where the agent runs commands, edits files, and is then graded. Our service is built on the open-source AgentENV project, to which we also contribute fixes. Between mid-September and mid-November, it ran about 944,000 sandboxes for this project, with up to 1,566 running concurrently . The service grew from one machine to as many as 12. We shipped ten upgrades to it, nearly all while training was running. Across all nine weeks, 99% of sandbox creations succeeded; since late October, that figure has exceeded 99.95%. Cloud infrastructure costs for the project’s sandboxes were about 80% lower than running the same sandboxes with popular cloud sandbox providers. One way we keep costs down is to let each sandbox’s memory allocation grow and shrink with its actual usage, allowing more sandboxes to share each machine. Try the model or train your own Download DaisyRose-27B , follow the SGLang serving guide , or use Miles to train your own agents. We’d like to hear how DaisyRose-27B performs on your tasks, including where it falls short. Share your setup and results in the model’s Community tab. We thank Eigent AI for working closely with us on training data, and the Qwen team for creating Qwen3.8-27B. We also thank the Miles and SGLang communities, along with other open-source projects including slime, AgentENV, and Harbor. Adapted from the original RadixArk article . items.content: Back to Articles Time-Series Models in the Streamhouse: A New Frontier and Use Cases Enterprise Article Published November 18, 2026 Upvote 34 +28 Nicholas Fuller nfuller Follow ibm-research Sean Falconer thefalc Follow ibm-research Ayhan Sebin ayhansebin Follow ibm-research Pankaj Dayama pankajdayama Follow ibm-research Roman Vaculin vaculin Follow ibm-research Bilge Zeren Aksu bzeren Follow ibm-research Julian Payne Pyjamacardinal Follow ibm-research Mountu Jinwala mjinwala Follow ibm-research Wesley M. Gifford wmgifford Follow ibm-research Chandra Reddy creddyhf Follow ibm-research Vijay Ekambaram vijaye12 Follow ibm-research Arindam Jati ajati Follow ibm-research Robert Metzger rmetzger0 Follow ibm-research Real-time forecasting, anomaly detection, and optimization, powered by IBM time-series models with more than 50 million downloads. Now available natively on Confluent, in the cloud and on premises, running on CPUs. Every business generates a continuous record of change: a machine reading, a payment, a sale, an order, or a change in inventory. These observations form time series, and they carry signals that can help teams anticipate what happens next. The challenge is turning those signals into decisions while they still matter. A forecast delivered after a production run, a stockout, or a payment authorization may be accurate, but too late to influence the outcome. IBM and Confluent are bringing time-series foundation models closer to the data as it flows. With Apache Flink, teams can apply forecasting , anomaly detection and semantic intelligence to streaming data using SQL, making model outputs available to the applications and people responsible for the next action. Foundation models have changed how organizations work with text, images, and documents. Time-series foundation models extend a similar idea to numerical data by learning general patterns from diverse historical data and then applying that knowledge to new series and tasks. The models can provide a starting point without requiring teams to train a separate model for every series. Depending on the task and deployment, teams can also fine-tune a model or combine its outputs with other data and business logic. Figure 1. More than 50 million downloads, and the family of four models behind them Now the time series foundation models run natively inside Confluent as built-in functions in the cloud and on premises. In Confluent Cloud they are fully managed, with nothing to deploy ( documentation ). On premises, the models can run within your own infrastructure using Confluent Platform for Apache Flink.( documentation ). The models run on CPUs, without requiring GPUs. The models can support a range of mission-critical use cases, from helping keep production lines in spec and detecting unusual store activity to improving product-level planning. They can also provide signals to assess card payments and forecast trading volume to help place large orders. These building blocks can be applied across manufacturing, retail, banking, and airlines, bringing insights closer to where decisions are made. See how time series and real-time context come together to create value: Streamhouse: real-time data and intelligence for agentic era Businesses operate continuously. Orders are updated, payments arrive, shipments are delayed, and inventory changes throughout the day. Yet the information behind these events often sits across systems that update at different times or rely on periodic batch processes. When applications and AI agents act on outdated or inconsistent information, they risk making decisions that no longer reflect what is happening. A Streamhouse addresses this by continuously capturing, processing, governing, and serving current business context. Confluent’s Data Streaming Platform brings together five capabilities—connect, stream, process, govern, and query—to make that context available to applications, analytics, and agents. Apache Flink transforms and enriches data as it flows, while Lightning Tables provide low-latency access to the current state. Figure 2. The Streamhouse on Confluent: from existing data sources to current business context that agents, applications, analytics and lakehouses use anywhere. Time-series models add predictive power to this architecture. Flink can prepare the data, invoke forecasting and anomaly detection, and make the results available alongside the events that produced them. Other models—including large language models, statistical models, and specialized machine learning systems—can contribute where appropriate. Figure 3. The intelligence layer of the Streamhouse: time series models, large language models, and ML and statistical models, with orchestration across them. This approach can help teams in four ways: - Scale model development . A pretrained model can provide a common starting point across many time series, reducing the need to develop and maintain a separate model for each one. - Refresh predictions as data changes . Forecasts can incorporate recent observations as part of a streaming workflow, subject to the model’s requirements and the pipeline’s configuration. - Put signals closer to decisions . Forecasts and anomalies can be routed to operational applications sooner, where teams can combine them with business context, rules, and human judgment. - Run compact models on CPUs. The models are small enough to run on standard CPUs alongside the streaming pipeline, in the cloud or on premises, which can reduce the need for dedicated GPU infrastructure and simplify deployment. Figure 4. Stream native time-series intelligence on Confluent Mission-critical use cases across real-enterprises The following scenarios illustrate how organizations could combine time-series models, streaming data, and application logic. Use Case 1 | Production optimization: every tub in spec An ice cream line’s quality depends on overrun—the amount of air whipped into the mix. Today, the process engineer and operator rely on QA lab measurements taken after the tubs are filled. If a new cream lot or a warm, humid day changes the process, hours of production may already need rework by the time the team sees the result. To get ahead of the problem, a pretrained TTM model reads SCADA telemetry and QA measurements every 10 minutes. It forecasts the share of tubs expected to be in spec four hours ahead, along with a likely range. When the forecast falls below the plant’s target, an optimization process evaluates combinations of freezer draw temperature and airflow. Because the model takes these control variables as inputs, it can score each option before anything changes on the line. The operator approves the recommended setpoints, while routine adjustments can be automated within predefined guardrails. The outcome is a more proactive process: less rework, lower energy use per tonne, and more consistent quality. The same approach can be applied to ovens, dryers, kilns, and mills. Figure 5. A forecast of product quality helps the operator evaluate freezer setpoints before making an adjustment. Use Case 2 | Anomaly detection: from a flag to the right action A store operations team monitors sales for thousands of products across hundreds of stores. Fixed thresholds often flag predictable weekend peaks while missing quieter changes, such as a product selling less than expected. As alerts accumulate, it becomes harder for the team to know where to focus. AI_DETECT_ANOMALIES gives each sales series an expected range based on its recent history. Each new reading is compared with that range at a confidence level the team chooses, without training a separate model for every product and store. When sales fall outside the expected range, the signal can be combined with inventory and store data to help identify a likely cause and recommend a next step—for example, checking the shelf or replenishing stock. The same approach can be applied to machine sensors, API telemetry, meter readings, and payment volumes. Figure 6. Store sales are compared with an expected range. In the view shown, recurring peaks remain within the range and no anomaly is flagged. Use Case 3 | Supply chain planning: every SKU, every store, every hour A category planner and a replenishment team need to keep products available across every store without carrying excess inventory. But forecasts may be refreshed only once a week, often focusing on top-selling products, while the long tail is managed with simpler rules. When sales patterns change between planning cycles, one store can run out while another has too much stock. With AI_FORECAST, a pretrained model can forecast demand across products and stores. In this example, it produces a 28-day forecast with a P10–P90 range, refreshed as new sales data arrives. The planning application combines the forecast with inventory, lead time, and the planner’s chosen service level to calculate a reorder point. When stock is projected to fall below that point, an agent can draft a purchase order for review. The same approach can support planning for spare parts, staffing, ATM cash, and energy demand. Figure 7. A store-level demand forecast informs a reorder point and a proposed purchase order for oat milk. Use Case 4 | Fraud and security: every card has its own normal Fraud teams already rely on sophisticated rules and models to evaluate transactions. One continuing challenge is that a threshold applied across many cardholders may not reflect how each person normally spends. A time-series signal can add that individual context. In this example, each payment is compared with an expected spending range based on the card’s recent history. A transaction outside that range is passed to the bank’s existing fraud systems as an additional input, alongside other signals and business rules. The bank can then decide whether to approve the payment, request additional authentication, or investigate further. The decision and the signals behind it can be retained for review. Figure 8.A payment outside the card’s expected spending range prompts a step-up authentication in an illustrative fraud workflow. Use Case 5 | Trading: pace the order with the tape An execution desk needs to divide a large order into smaller trades while managing its effect on the market. Historical volume curves offer a starting point, but today’s trading activity may look very different from the average. On each one-minute bar, PatchTST-FM forecasts trading volume for the next 30 minutes, with a P10–P90 range. The execution algorithm uses that forecast to pace the order within the participation limit set by the desk. If a news event changes market activity, the algorithm can pause and replan. If trading is quieter than expected, it can reduce the size of each slice and signal that the order may take longer to complete. Each forecast and the resulting execution decisions can be retained in the audit trail. Figure 9. Volume forecast informs the proposed execution schedule for a 100,000-share order. Use Case 6 | Semantic search: find every signal that looks like this A reliability engineer investigating an unusual sensor pattern may want to know whether similar behavior appeared elsewhere in the plant. TSPulse can produce representations of time-series windows that support similarity search. In a separately built application, those representations could be indexed and used to retrieve historical patterns across equipment. An engineer could search for shapes such as a spike and recovery, a gradual rise, or a step change, then inspect the associated maintenance records and operating conditions. This application requires an embedding pipeline, an index, and access to the relevant context. Similarity can help narrow an investigation; it does not establish a root cause by itself. Figure 10. Time-series embeddings can support a search for similar patterns across equipment and other signals. Industry Specific Applications The same models and building blocks can support different workflows across industries: Industrial AI: from sensor to setpoint. The plant manager wants every batch in spec and no line stopped by a surprise. SCADA, QA lab and energy meter streams are forecast as they arrive. Production optimization moves the setpoints when quality starts to drift, anomaly detection flags the reading no rule was written for, and semantic search finds every pump that showed the same pattern before a failure. Setpoints, work orders and alerts reach the floor inside the cycle, not at the next shift report. Figure 11. The plant twin, from sensor to setpoint. A new cream lot pulls overrun off target. The forecast reads the line, the agent proposes a new draw temperature and air flow, the operator approves, and the tubs are back in spec. Simulated data. Retail: a store and its supply chain. The store manager wants a full shelf on Saturday without overstock on Monday. Sales, weather and promotion streams are forecast for every product in every store. Supply chain planning sets the order, anomaly detection catches the empty shelf or the missed delivery, and fraud and security holds the suspicious card. Orders, store tasks and holds go out before the shelf runs empty. Figure 12. The store twin, a store and its supply chain. A promo is coming for oat milk. The forecast prices in the promo and sets the reorder point, the agent raises a purchase order, the planner approves, and the shelf is full on promo day. Simulated data. Banking: payments and the trading desk. The fraud lead wants to stop card testing without blocking good customers, and the trader wants a large order done without moving the price. Every card and every symbol is scored against its own expected pattern, event by event. Fraud and security holds the odd swipe before authorization, anomaly detection spots the unusual flow, and trading paces each order with the forecast volume. Airlines: hub operations, fleet and network. Operations control wants to see a disruption coming while there is still time to act. Engine, gate and network streams are forecast and checked in real time. Anomaly detection catches the engine reading that drifts, production optimization rebalances gates and crews, and supply chain planning puts the spare part where the aircraft will be. items.raw_text: Back to Articles Time-Series Models in the Streamhouse: A New Frontier and Use Cases Enterprise Article Published November 18, 2026 Upvote 34 +28 Nicholas Fuller nfuller Follow ibm-research Sean Falconer thefalc Follow ibm-research Ayhan Sebin ayhansebin Follow ibm-research Pankaj Dayama pankajdayama Follow ibm-research Roman Vaculin vaculin Follow ibm-research Bilge Zeren Aksu bzeren Follow ibm-research Julian Payne Pyjamacardinal Follow ibm-research Mountu Jinwala mjinwala Follow ibm-research Wesley M. Gifford wmgifford Follow ibm-research Chandra Reddy creddyhf Follow ibm-research Vijay Ekambaram vijaye12 Follow ibm-research Arindam Jati ajati Follow ibm-research Robert Metzger rmetzger0 Follow ibm-research Real-time forecasting, anomaly detection, and optimization, powered by IBM time-series models with more than 50 million downloads. Now available natively on Confluent, in the cloud and on premises, running on CPUs. Every business generates a continuous record of change: a machine reading, a payment, a sale, an order, or a change in inventory. These observations form time series, and they carry signals that can help teams anticipate what happens next. The challenge is turning those signals into decisions while they still matter. A forecast delivered after a production run, a stockout, or a payment authorization may be accurate, but too late to influence the outcome. IBM and Confluent are bringing time-series foundation models closer to the data as it flows. With Apache Flink, teams can apply forecasting , anomaly detection and semantic intelligence to streaming data using SQL, making model outputs available to the applications and people responsible for the next action. Foundation models have changed how organizations work with text, images, and documents. Time-series foundation models extend a similar idea to numerical data by learning general patterns from diverse historical data and then applying that knowledge to new series and tasks. The models can provide a starting point without requiring teams to train a separate model for every series. Depending on the task and deployment, teams can also fine-tune a model or combine its outputs with other data and business logic. Figure 1. More than 50 million downloads, and the family of four models behind them Now the time series foundation models run natively inside Confluent as built-in functions in the cloud and on premises. In Confluent Cloud they are fully managed, with nothing to deploy ( documentation ). On premises, the models can run within your own infrastructure using Confluent Platform for Apache Flink.( documentation ). The models run on CPUs, without requiring GPUs. The models can support a range of mission-critical use cases, from helping keep production lines in spec and detecting unusual store activity to improving product-level planning. They can also provide signals to assess card payments and forecast trading volume to help place large orders. These building blocks can be applied across manufacturing, retail, banking, and airlines, bringing insights closer to where decisions are made. See how time series and real-time context come together to create value: Streamhouse: real-time data and intelligence for agentic era Businesses operate continuously. Orders are updated, payments arrive, shipments are delayed, and inventory changes throughout the day. Yet the information behind these events often sits across systems that update at different times or rely on periodic batch processes. When applications and AI agents act on outdated or inconsistent information, they risk making decisions that no longer reflect what is happening. A Streamhouse addresses this by continuously capturing, processing, governing, and serving current business context. Confluent’s Data Streaming Platform brings together five capabilities—connect, stream, process, govern, and query—to make that context available to applications, analytics, and agents. Apache Flink transforms and enriches data as it flows, while Lightning Tables provide low-latency access to the current state. Figure 2. The Streamhouse on Confluent: from existing data sources to current business context that agents, applications, analytics and lakehouses use anywhere. Time-series models add predictive power to this architecture. Flink can prepare the data, invoke forecasting and anomaly detection, and make the results available alongside the events that produced them. Other models—including large language models, statistical models, and specialized machine learning systems—can contribute where appropriate. Figure 3. The intelligence layer of the Streamhouse: time series models, large language models, and ML and statistical models, with orchestration across them. This approach can help teams in four ways: - Scale model development . A pretrained model can provide a common starting point across many time series, reducing the need to develop and maintain a separate model for each one. - Refresh predictions as data changes . Forecasts can incorporate recent observations as part of a streaming workflow, subject to the model’s requirements and the pipeline’s configuration. - Put signals closer to decisions . Forecasts and anomalies can be routed to operational applications sooner, where teams can combine them with business context, rules, and human judgment. - Run compact models on CPUs. The models are small enough to run on standard CPUs alongside the streaming pipeline, in the cloud or on premises, which can reduce the need for dedicated GPU infrastructure and simplify deployment. Figure 4. Stream native time-series intelligence on Confluent Mission-critical use cases across real-enterprises The following scenarios illustrate how organizations could combine time-series models, streaming data, and application logic. Use Case 1 | Production optimization: every tub in spec An ice cream line’s quality depends on overrun—the amount of air whipped into the mix. Today, the process engineer and operator rely on QA lab measurements taken after the tubs are filled. If a new cream lot or a warm, humid day changes the process, hours of production may already need rework by the time the team sees the result. To get ahead of the problem, a pretrained TTM model reads SCADA telemetry and QA measurements every 10 minutes. It forecasts the share of tubs expected to be in spec four hours ahead, along with a likely range. When the forecast falls below the plant’s target, an optimization process evaluates combinations of freezer draw temperature and airflow. Because the model takes these control variables as inputs, it can score each option before anything changes on the line. The operator approves the recommended setpoints, while routine adjustments can be automated within predefined guardrails. The outcome is a more proactive process: less rework, lower energy use per tonne, and more consistent quality. The same approach can be applied to ovens, dryers, kilns, and mills. Figure 5. A forecast of product quality helps the operator evaluate freezer setpoints before making an adjustment. Use Case 2 | Anomaly detection: from a flag to the right action A store operations team monitors sales for thousands of products across hundreds of stores. Fixed thresholds often flag predictable weekend peaks while missing quieter changes, such as a product selling less than expected. As alerts accumulate, it becomes harder for the team to know where to focus. AI_DETECT_ANOMALIES gives each sales series an expected range based on its recent history. Each new reading is compared with that range at a confidence level the team chooses, without training a separate model for every product and store. When sales fall outside the expected range, the signal can be combined with inventory and store data to help identify a likely cause and recommend a next step—for example, checking the shelf or replenishing stock. The same approach can be applied to machine sensors, API telemetry, meter readings, and payment volumes. Figure 6. Store sales are compared with an expected range. In the view shown, recurring peaks remain within the range and no anomaly is flagged. Use Case 3 | Supply chain planning: every SKU, every store, every hour A category planner and a replenishment team need to keep products available across every store without carrying excess inventory. But forecasts may be refreshed only once a week, often focusing on top-selling products, while the long tail is managed with simpler rules. When sales patterns change between planning cycles, one store can run out while another has too much stock. With AI_FORECAST, a pretrained model can forecast demand across products and stores. In this example, it produces a 28-day forecast with a P10–P90 range, refreshed as new sales data arrives. The planning application combines the forecast with inventory, lead time, and the planner’s chosen service level to calculate a reorder point. When stock is projected to fall below that point, an agent can draft a purchase order for review. The same approach can support planning for spare parts, staffing, ATM cash, and energy demand. Figure 7. A store-level demand forecast informs a reorder point and a proposed purchase order for oat milk. Use Case 4 | Fraud and security: every card has its own normal Fraud teams already rely on sophisticated rules and models to evaluate transactions. One continuing challenge is that a threshold applied across many cardholders may not reflect how each person normally spends. A time-series signal can add that individual context. In this example, each payment is compared with an expected spending range based on the card’s recent history. A transaction outside that range is passed to the bank’s existing fraud systems as an additional input, alongside other signals and business rules. The bank can then decide whether to approve the payment, request additional authentication, or investigate further. The decision and the signals behind it can be retained for review. Figure 8.A payment outside the card’s expected spending range prompts a step-up authentication in an illustrative fraud workflow. Use Case 5 | Trading: pace the order with the tape An execution desk needs to divide a large order into smaller trades while managing its effect on the market. Historical volume curves offer a starting point, but today’s trading activity may look very different from the average. On each one-minute bar, PatchTST-FM forecasts trading volume for the next 30 minutes, with a P10–P90 range. The execution algorithm uses that forecast to pace the order within the participation limit set by the desk. If a news event changes market activity, the algorithm can pause and replan. If trading is quieter than expected, it can reduce the size of each slice and signal that the order may take longer to complete. Each forecast and the resulting execution decisions can be retained in the audit trail. Figure 9. Volume forecast informs the proposed execution schedule for a 100,000-share order. Use Case 6 | Semantic search: find every signal that looks like this A reliability engineer investigating an unusual sensor pattern may want to know whether similar behavior appeared elsewhere in the plant. TSPulse can produce representations of time-series windows that support similarity search. In a separately built application, those representations could be indexed and used to retrieve historical patterns across equipment. An engineer could search for shapes such as a spike and recovery, a gradual rise, or a step change, then inspect the associated maintenance records and operating conditions. This application requires an embedding pipeline, an index, and access to the relevant context. Similarity can help narrow an investigation; it does not establish a root cause by itself. Figure 10. Time-series embeddings can support a search for similar patterns across equipment and other signals. Industry Specific Applications The same models and building blocks can support different workflows across industries: Industrial AI: from sensor to setpoint. The plant manager wants every batch in spec and no line stopped by a surprise. SCADA, QA lab and energy meter streams are forecast as they arrive. Production optimization moves the setpoints when quality starts to drift, anomaly detection flags the reading no rule was written for, and semantic search finds every pump that showed the same pattern before a failure. Setpoints, work orders and alerts reach the floor inside the cycle, not at the next shift report. Figure 11. The plant twin, from sensor to setpoint. A new cream lot pulls overrun off target. The forecast reads the line, the agent proposes a new draw temperature and air flow, the operator approves, and the tubs are back in spec. Simulated data. Retail: a store and its supply chain. The store manager wants a full shelf on Saturday without overstock on Monday. Sales, weather and promotion streams are forecast for every product in every store. Supply chain planning sets the order, anomaly detection catches the empty shelf or the missed delivery, and fraud and security holds the suspicious card. Orders, store tasks and holds go out before the shelf runs empty. Figure 12. The store twin, a store and its supply chain. A promo is coming for oat milk. The forecast prices in the promo and sets the reorder point, the agent raises a purchase order, the planner approves, and the shelf is full on promo day. Simulated data. Banking: payments and the trading desk. The fraud lead wants to stop card testing without blocking good customers, and the trader wants a large order done without moving the price. Every card and every symbol is scored against its own expected pattern, event by event. Fraud and security holds the odd swipe before authorization, anomaly detection spots the unusual flow, and trading paces each order with the forecast volume. Airlines: hub operations, fleet and network. Operations control wants to see a disruption coming while there is still time to act. Engine, gate and network streams are forecast and checked in real time. Anomaly detection catches the engine reading that drifts, production optimization rebalances gates and crews, and supply chain planning puts the spare part where the aircraft will be. items.content: Back to Articles 180B Parameters, 32GB of RAM: Pushing MoE Inference to the Limit with Transformers Published November 18, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 33 +27 Tarek Ziadé tarekziade Follow Streaming MoE experts directly from SSD gets within 6% of Strata on token generation. I've been trying to rely less on online models and run bigger ones locally. At home I have a PC with two RTX 4090s (let's call it Orthrus - the two-headed hound of Greek mythology), and for work I have a MacBook M5 with 32G of unified memory. Orthrus runs on Windows 11, because my kids play games all the time. I had a dual boot with Ubuntu, but their games ended up taking most of the two terabytes of disk. I am also a huge fan of RMD (rooms moving development): one hour in the kitchen sipping my coffee, two hours at my office desk, then the sofa. A fixed desktop tower is not for me. My first experiment was to run Qwen 3.8 27B with llama.app on Orthrus and use it from my laptop through pi . That model does the coding tasks, an online model like Opus does the orchestration, and the second RTX runs a FIM model for auto-completion in Neovim. When I talked about this on social networks, I got very strong feedback: use Strata with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next . What is Strata? Strata is an inference engine for MoE models like Qwen. Only the hot experts stay in VRAM, the rest goes to RAM, or even to disk. Experts are 90%+ of a MoE model's weights, so a 180B model like this one can run on a GPU with much less memory. Like my RTX 4090! It works on a laptop too, and I stumbled on this blog post doing exactly that: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac M4, faster than llama.cpp , at 13.5 tok/s. That's too slow for how I use coding agents, but it's an interesting itch to scratch. A whole range of MoE models don't fit in a MacBook's unified memory and could run at a decent speed. How do other engines offload? Before committing to Strata, I looked at what llama.cpp, vLLM and Transformers do when a MoE model doesn't fit. Three questions matter: where do the experts live, where does the expert matmul run, and what moves on each token? llama.cpp maps the GGUF file with mmap and can keep the experts on the CPU ( --cpu-moe , --n-cpu-moe N , -ot "exps=CPU" , or --fit on to pick for you). Those experts are also computed on the CPU, so only the activations cross PCIe, never the weights. Great when the experts fit in RAM. When they don't, the page cache thrashes. A GPU expert cache ( --moe-cache-mib ) just landed, but it fragments the graph (2 splits per token become 50) and loses ~10% even when everything fits. vLLM 's --cpu-offload-gb N puts N GB of weights in pinned RAM, and kernels read them in place over PCIe. For a MoE layer, that's only the routed experts, but nothing is cached: a hot expert crosses PCIe again on every token, and there's no disk tier. By default the offloaded weights include dense layers, read on every token; --cpu-offload-params experts keeps it to the experts. That fits vLLM's big batches, which touch almost every expert anyway, less so one user on one GPU. Transformers offloads through Accelerate ( device_map="auto" , offload_folder ), one module at a time: hooks copy its weights to the GPU before forward . For a MoE, that module is a layer's whole expert bank, so every token copies every expert of every offloaded layer to use 8 or 10 of them. No cache, no notion of routing. And on a Mac, CPU and GPU share the same memory, so "offload to CPU" frees nothing. I ran all of them on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on one A10G (24 GB), with plenty of RAM, and Harry Mellor reran vLLM with better flags: Engine Decode (tok/s) Strata, Q8_0 82 - 88 llama.cpp, Q8_0, --fit on 63 - 64 llama.cpp, BF16, --fit on 35 - 36 vLLM, FP8, --cpu-offload-gb 16 --cpu-offload-params experts 20.1 vLLM, FP8, same flags, --enforce-eager 14.7 vLLM, FP8, --cpu-offload-gb 16 9.7 vLLM, BF16, --cpu-offload-gb 50 --cpu-offload-params experts 7.3 vLLM, BF16, --cpu-offload-gb 50 3.3 Transformers + Accelerate 0.16 Offloading only the experts doubles vLLM's speed, and FP8 helps on top (half the bytes per expert, more of the model on the GPU). vLLM's other offload backend, which copies groups of layers ahead of time, ran under 1 tok/s. If the experts fit in RAM, llama.cpp is hard to beat. If they don't, you have to stream only what the router picks, through a bounded cache, fast enough that the SSD is the bottleneck and not Python, ideally reusing the model's fast expert kernels. That's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac, and Transformers couldn't do it out of the box. Making Qwen3.8-Flash-Next work on my 32 GB Mac with Transformers Strata was already too slow for me on the laptop, and Transformers was not going to beat it anytime soon. But the Accelerate path was so far off that I wanted to try fixing offloading in Transformers itself, with the big model on my laptop as the target, knowing it would probably stay too slow for how I work. All of the code was built with AI: the Transformers PR, the model-specific package and the Metal kernels. My part was choosing what to try, reading the profiles, and deciding what to keep. Everything is in a Space: tarekziade/moe-expert-streaming . Start small I started with OLMoE-1B-7B , which fits in memory, so I could compare every token with vanilla Transformers. First version: experts on disk, an LRU cache on the device, and a Python loop running one expert at a time. With every expert already cached, it did 10.1 tok/s. Vanilla did ~32. The I/O was fine, my loop was not: vanilla uses grouped_mm , which runs all the experts of a layer in one kernel. The fix, and the key idea of this project, was to turn the cache into a slot pool : one preallocated device tensor shared by all layers, plus a per-layer table from expert id to slot. Remap the router's expert ids to slots and the pool looks like a regular expert bank, so grouped_mm runs on it as is. No custom expert matmul needed. That got it to 34.6 tok/s, against 38.1 for vanilla. experts_offload I then turned the standalone loader into an option of from_pretrained , in huggingface/transformers#50717 . To try it, install Transformers from that PR: pip install "git+https://github.com/huggingface/transformers.git@refs/pull/50717/head" Then, moving from OLMoE to the real target, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next: path = snapshot_download( "tarekziade/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-expert-streaming" ) model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( f" {path} /dense" , dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map={ "" : "mps" , "experts.*" : "disk" }, quantization_config=MetalConfig(bits= 8 ), experts_offload={ "cache_bytes" : 12 << 30 , "quantized_experts" : f" {path} /experts-q3" , }, ) That repo holds the output of the project's conversion script : the dense weights, the experts quantized to 3 bits, and the n-gram table. Experts mapped to "disk" go through the streaming path instead of Accelerate's offload: the loader skips their tensors and MoE layers switch to an offloaded implementation. Misses are read by 8 I/O threads, one contiguous read per expert. The next two layers' routers run early on the current hidden states to guess which experts to prefetch. Experts can be quantized offline so reads are smaller. It works for MoE models with the standard experts layout. The API is still being discussed with the Transformers maintainers. The device_map form came out of that, and quantized experts will probably go through the per-layer quantization plan of #50245 rather than their own option. Running 121 GB of experts on a 32 GB Mac Qwen3.8-Flash-Next has 48 layers of 512 experts (10 active), 121 GB in FP8. Streaming them isn't enough: there's also a 51 GB n-gram embedding table that needs its own disk path. So: experts quantized to 3 bits: 49 GB on disk, 12 GiB cached on the device dense layers in 8 bits (~5.4 GB, +0.2% perplexity vs BF16) the n-gram table stays on disk, rows read when needed The conversion takes ~5 hours. After loading, it uses ~18 GiB, and a 6K prompt peaks at 25.4 GiB. That's about the limit: I have to close the browser, or macOS starts swapping. The model-specific bits (the n-gram table, Metal kernels) live in a small package, moe-expert-streaming , on top of the PR. The first version ran at about 10 tok/s. Then I installed Strata on the same M5, with the same prompts: Transformers Strata Gap Decode, 200 tokens 10.0 tok/s 14.8 1.5x Prefill, 4K prompt 68 tok/s 220 3.2x Decode after a 6K document 7.3 tok/s 13.7 1.9x Strata 0.1.60 used IQ3_XXS experts. Both ran greedy, with thinking, MTP and speculative drafts off, and 1,024-token prefill chunks. The full setup and raw results are on the Space's details page . I also tried vllm-metal , vLLM on Apple GPUs through MLX, which recently got expert offloading. It streams the routed experts from an MLX checkpoint through a bounded cache, like this project. But it can't run Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on 32 GB, for the n-gram reason above: only the experts are streamed, and the n-gram tables stay in memory. That's 32 GB in the MLX checkpoints on the Hub, before the ~5 GB of dense layers and any expert cache. Closing the gap Most of the time wasn't spent on experts. Here's what helped: Committing GPU work early. PyTorch on MPS holds small kernels until the next sync, so the GPU idled while Python worked. Forcing a commit after each block gave +10%. This should really be fixed in PyTorch. Metal kernels for the parts without a fast path on macOS: Gated DeltaNet and the hyper-connections. Strata's own weights. I switched to Strata's GGUF weights , reducing dense weight traffic from 5.4 GB to 3.9 GB per token and individual expert size from 2.15 MB to 1.75 MB, with a separate cache pool for each expert size. Prefill , we went from 68 to ~228 tok/s using bigger chunks, and reading the next layer's experts while the current layer is being computed. Long documents : attention over the indexer's selected blocks only, and a KV cache that grows in place instead of being copied at every token. Misses : Strata doesn't hide them, it waits like I do, and no cache policy beat LRU by much. What helped was reading just one guessed expert per layer, while the SSD would otherwise be idle. Here's one MoE layer for one token, as it runs now: These are the final results after these optimizations on the same M5 with the same prompts: Transformers Strata Gap Decode, 200 tokens 13.9 tok/s 14.8 1.06x Prefill, 4K prompt 228 tok/s 220 1.0x Decode after a 6K document 12.4 tok/s 13.7 1.1x That's about 6% behind Strata on short decode, with slightly faster prefill, all through Transformers. Most of what's left is host round trips, ~10 ms per token. Waking up after a sync is only ~1 ms of that. The rest is the GPU running dry while Python queues the next layer. Strata queues the whole token's work up front, and the GPU waits on a Metal shared event at each layer while the host reads experts. PyTorch doesn't expose that. I tried to fake it with a kernel spinning on a flag the CPU writes, and the GPU took anywhere from a second to never to see the write. The real fix would be a native op on PyTorch's MPS stream, with a risk of hangs, so I haven't built it. Conclusion It runs at ~14 tok/s, close to Strata, and it's still too slow for how I use coding agents. Orthrus keeps doing the real work. Transformers didn't beat Strata, and closing the last ~6% would take deeper changes in the stack, starting with control over that per-layer sync, which PyTorch doesn't give you today. The interesting part is how it got that close: streaming only the routed experts, a bounded cache that grouped_mm runs on as is, and a few targeted Metal kernels. There's no C++ extension in the project: just Python, Metal kernels compiled at runtime with torch.mps.compile_shader , and prebuilt kernels from the Hub . All the Metal kernels written for this experiment are now published on the Hub , and the project loads them from there. Beating Strata was never the only goal, though. Building this was a great way to learn how MoEs and LLMs work from a systems perspective: how sparse the routing really is, how much an expert cache buys you, where memory bandwidth goes per token, and how much time the host and the GPU spend waiting on each other. Transformers makes all of that easy to poke at, one module at a time. The generic expert streaming implementation is in huggingface/transformers#50717 , and the benchmarks are in the Space . Feedback on the approach and the API is welcome. Thanks to Pedro, Lysandre and Arthur for their excellent feedback, and to Harry for helping test vLLM. Finally, thanks to Niko Veit for Strata . Strata set the bar for what's possible with expert streaming on consumer hardware, and having those numbers to chase is what pushed this work as far as it went.
